opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic worry is something like this. A lot of the work that gets labeled "alignment research" is also just work that makes AI systems more useful. If you figure out how to get a model to reliably do what its operator wants, follow instructions, not make embarrassing mistakes, that's a big part of what makes the system commercially valuable. RLHF is maybe the clearest example. I worked on it, and I think it was a reasonable thing to do. But it also made language models much more usable products, and that plausibly increased investment and sped things up.

So when you ask whether alignment work could be net negative, the question is roughly: how much does it help us handle the risk, versus how much does it accelerate the arrival of powerful systems? If it mostly accelerates things and only slightly helps, then you've given up time you could have spent on safety, and that's bad.

My overall view is that most alignment work is positive on net, for a few reasons. First, the commercial incentive to make systems useful is enormous. If alignment researchers didn't develop some technique, a lot of that would get built anyway, maybe a bit later and maybe less carefully. So the counterfactual acceleration is often smaller than it looks. Second, the alternative to having these techniques isn't that people don't deploy AI. It's that they deploy systems we understand worse. Third, a lot of the most important alignment work, like interpretability, scalable oversight, or understanding when models might deceive us, isn't that useful commercially in the near term. That's the stuff that's really differential.

But I do take the concern seriously. I'd want people to think about it at the margin. If your research is mostly making systems more capable and the safety benefit is speculative, I'd be more worried. If it's the kind of thing that only matters once systems are really powerful and may otherwise be trying to undermine oversight, that's more clearly good. And I'd add that time itself isn't automatically valuable. Extra time is only good if people are actually using it to make progress on the hard problems, and that's a lot of why I think doing the research now still matters.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment research can be net negative when it mostly accelerates AI and provides little safety benefit. It does not state that acceleration alone could not make it net negative if the only reason to slow progress is to gain alignment research time.

r002.rationale: The response explains that acceleration can reduce time available for safety work: if the research mostly speeds progress and only slightly helps, it has given up time that could have been spent on safety.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the question is kind of pointing at a real tension, and I want to be careful about how I decompose it. There's one claim, which is that alignment research is good. There's a second claim, which is that slowing down AI progress is good because it gives you more time. And then there's a question of whether those two things are actually in tension with each other, which I think they can be.

So the most straightforward way that alignment research could be net negative is just that a lot of alignment research also makes AI systems more useful. If I figure out how to get a model to do what I want, that's alignment, but it's also capabilities in the sense that now the model is more economically valuable, people deploy it more, more money flows into the field, and the whole thing accelerates. RLHF is the obvious example. I worked on that, and I think it was reasonable to work on, but I also think it's fair to say that it made language models dramatically more useful and probably pulled forward the timeline on which people got excited about them and invested in them. So if you think that acceleration is bad, you have to weigh that against whatever safety benefit you got.

Now, I don't actually think that's the dominant consideration for most alignment work. I think for most of what I'd call alignment research, the capabilities externality is pretty small, and the main effect is just that you understand the systems better or you have better techniques for controlling them. But I do think people should take it seriously as a cost rather than pretending it's zero.

The second way it could be net negative is a bit more subtle, and it's something like: alignment research can make people feel safer than they should. If you have a bunch of techniques that work fine on current systems, and everyone kind of nods and says, okay, we've got alignment handled, then that can reduce the pressure for the kind of caution that you'd actually want. And then when you get to systems where those techniques stop working, you've already built up a lot of momentum and a lot of institutional confidence. So in some sense, partial solutions can be worse than no solution, if they're mistaken for full solutions.

I think that one's real but it's also kind of a general argument against doing anything useful, right? Like, any safety measure can give false confidence. So the response has to be to do the research but also be really honest about what it does and doesn't cover, rather than to not do the research.

And then the last piece is just about what "more time" actually buys you. I think the value of slowing down depends a lot on whether the time gets used well. If you slow down and nobody does alignment research during that time, you've gained basically nothing. If you slow down and people do alignment research, then the slowing down is good precisely because the research is good. So I'd push back a little on framing these as alternatives. I think the case for slowing down is largely a case for giving alignment research time to work, and so if you believe in slowing down, you should generally also believe that alignment research is valuable. The place where they come apart is just the specific projects that have large capabilities spillovers, and there I think you have to make a judgment call project by project.

My overall view is that alignment research is pretty robustly positive, that there's a minority of it where the acceleration effect is large enough that it's a close call, and that the right response to that is to be thoughtful about which problems you work on and how you publish, not to conclude that the whole enterprise is net negative.

r001.rationale: The response says slowing down can give alignment research time to work and that alignment research is generally valuable, but it does not state that alignment research cannot be net negative solely because it accelerates progress when gaining that time is the only reason to slow down. It also says some projects may be close calls.

r002.rationale: The response explains that alignment work can make AI more useful and accelerate investment and deployment, but it does not say this acceleration reduces time available for other forms of AI safety preparedness.

astra-6.text:
Well, slowing down AI progress isn’t necessarily what alignment research does. A lot of alignment research makes AI systems more useful. If you can get a model to reliably do what you want, that’s both an alignment improvement and a reason to deploy that model more widely or invest more in developing the next one.

So you have to compare two effects. How much does the work reduce the risk from a given level of capability, and how much does it accelerate getting to more dangerous capabilities? In principle, the second effect could be larger.

There’s also a question of which problems you’re solving. You could make systems behave much better in the situations we can test today, without making much progress on whether much smarter systems will remain aligned. If that makes people more confident and speeds up deployment, you may have shortened the time available to solve the harder problem.

I don’t think that means alignment research is generally bad. It means you need a more specific argument than ‘this makes AI behave better, therefore it reduces existential risk.’ You need to ask what happens downstream of the particular research you’re doing.

r001.rationale: The response says acceleration could outweigh risk reduction, but does not state that acceleration alone would not make alignment research net negative if gaining time were the only reason to slow progress.

r002.rationale: It explains that research can speed deployment and thereby shorten the time available to solve the harder alignment problem in more capable systems.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, alignment research doesn’t necessarily slow down AI progress. A lot of it makes AI systems more useful. If you make a model better at following instructions, or better at doing what a human evaluator wants, that can accelerate the development and deployment of AI. And it can potentially help automate AI research itself.

So you have to ask what you’re getting in exchange for that acceleration. Are you solving the problems that would otherwise cause us to lose control of very powerful systems? Or are you mostly solving problems that make today’s systems commercially useful, while leaving the hard problems for later?

There’s also a possibility of giving people more confidence than is warranted. You could make systems look much better under the kinds of evaluations we can do today without making them much safer in the situations that ultimately matter.

I don’t think that means alignment research is generally bad. It means you need to evaluate particular research directions by how much they improve our ability to handle the dangerous part of AI development, relative to how much they accelerate us toward it.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment research can accelerate AI progress and calls for weighing that acceleration against safety benefits, but it does not state that acceleration alone cannot make the research net negative when the only reason for slowing progress is to gain alignment time.

r002.rationale: It warns that research may accelerate AI while leaving hard problems for later, but does not explain that this acceleration reduces time for other forms of AI safety preparedness.
